opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea is pretty simple. Suppose that as an agent works through a task, at every step, or every minute of human-equivalent work, there's some fixed probability that it makes an unrecoverable mistake. If that hazard rate is constant, the probability of completing the whole task decays exponentially with task length. You get a survival curve, like radioactive decay, and you can describe the model's ability with a half-life: the task length at which it succeeds about half the time.

What's appealing is that it's a one-parameter description. In our time horizon work, we measure how long tasks take skilled humans, then look at model success rates across lengths. We fit a logistic curve rather than strictly assuming an exponential, but the constant failure rate story is a nice intuition for why success falls off smoothly with length instead of dropping off a cliff. Toby Ord wrote about this framing, and it fits the data surprisingly well.

It also tells you something about what's improving. If each new generation roughly halves its per-step error rate, its horizon roughly doubles, which is a mechanistic story for the exponential trend we see in time horizons.

That said, I don't think it's literally true. Real tasks aren't uniform: some steps are much harder than others, models can sometimes notice and recover from errors, and failures cluster around certain bottlenecks. Humans especially don't have a constant hazard rate; their success curves are flatter because they backtrack and fix things. So one interesting question is whether models start looking more human-like, with a decreasing hazard rate, as they get better at error correction. If so, the simple exponential picture would underestimate how far they can go on long tasks. So I see it as a useful baseline model, a good first approximation, rather than the final word.

r001.rationale: The response describes a fixed failure rate during a task and notes that task steps can vary in difficulty, but it does not state that different tasks may have different failure rates.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea is pretty simple. Imagine that at every step of a task, there's some fixed probability that the model makes a mistake it can't recover from. Call it a constant hazard rate. If that's the case, then the probability of successfully finishing a task decays exponentially with how many steps the task requires. So a task that takes ten steps, you're fine; a task that takes a hundred steps, you're much less likely to get through without hitting one of those unrecoverable errors.

What's nice about this is it gives you a really clean model that connects task length to success rate. And it's basically the model that METR used when they put out their task horizon work, where they measure how long a task a model can complete at fifty percent reliability, with length measured by how long it takes a human expert to do it. If you fit a logistic curve of success rate against log task length, that's roughly what you'd expect to get from a constant failure rate per unit of time.

And empirically, that curve fits surprisingly well. I think a lot of people, me included, expected it to be messier, because tasks differ in all sorts of ways beyond just length. But length turns out to explain a lot of the variance.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't think the constant failure rate is literally true as a mechanistic story about what's going on inside the model. It's more like a useful first-order approximation. Real tasks aren't a chain of independent, identically risky steps. Some steps are way harder than others. Sometimes the model can notice it made a mistake and fix it, which breaks the "unrecoverable" assumption. And if you look closely at how models fail on long tasks, a lot of the time it's not some random slip at step forty-seven. It's more like they lose track of what they were doing, or they get confused about the state of the environment, or they keep trying the same wrong thing. Those failures feel more correlated with context length and with the structure of the task than with a per-step coin flip.

So the way I think about it is: the constant failure rate model is good for extrapolating trends and for giving you a single number, like the fifty percent horizon, that you can track over time. That's really valuable, especially for forecasting. But if you want to understand why models fail, or predict performance on a specific kind of task, you need to go a level deeper. You want to know things like, how well does the model recover from errors, how well does it maintain a plan over a long context, how does it handle when the environment gives it ambiguous feedback. Those are the things that actually determine whether the effective failure rate goes down as models get better.

And I think that's actually the more interesting question going forward. The horizon numbers have been doubling on something like a seven-month timescale. Whether that continues depends a lot on whether labs figure out how to make models that catch and correct their own mistakes, because that's the thing that would most directly break the exponential decay story in a good way. If you can recover from errors, then the per-step failure stops compounding the same way, and long tasks become much more feasible.

r001.rationale: The response describes a fixed failure probability per step and notes that tasks differ in difficulty, but it does not state that the model may assign different constant failure rates to different tasks.

astra-6.text:
One way to think about it is that a task requires a sequence of steps, and at each step the model has some probability of making a mistake it can’t recover from. If that probability is roughly constant, then the probability of successfully completing the whole task falls exponentially with the number of steps.

So you could have a model that’s very reliable on each individual step, and looks quite impressive on short tasks, but still struggles with longer tasks. And improving that per-step reliability would let it complete longer tasks without necessarily giving it some fundamentally new capability.

The constant failure rate is obviously a simplifying assumption. Some steps are harder than others, failures can be correlated, and models can sometimes recover from mistakes. But it gives you a useful baseline for thinking about how performance might change with task length.

r001.rationale: The response describes a roughly constant per-step failure probability and how task length affects success. It notes that some steps are harder, but does not state that the model may assign different failure rates to different tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
One simple model is to imagine that, at every step of a task, the model has some fixed probability of making a mistake that causes it to fail. If that probability is p, and the task takes n steps, then its probability of succeeding is roughly (1 − p) to the n. So even a model that’s very reliable on individual steps can struggle with a sufficiently long task.

I think that’s a useful baseline for thinking about task length. Improving the per-step failure rate lets you do longer tasks at the same overall reliability. But the constant failure rate is an assumption, and you’d want to test it. Errors could be correlated, some steps could be much harder than others, and a system might notice and recover from mistakes. So I’d treat it as a simple model to compare against, rather than a claim about how AI systems necessarily behave.
